title: "Muhammad is His messenger"
hook: the second half accepts the Prophet ﷺ as the one who shows how

segments.voice: Yesterday, but Allah, illallah, and your line: then, yes. After you turned something down, what did you turn toward? Today, the second sentence. Day one thousand sixty-six.

Nobody learns to tie a knot from a paragraph. You watch somebody's hands, slowly, then try it, then watch again. The first sentence of the shahadah says there is one God to worship. It leaves a practical question hanging in the air: fine, but how? How do you pray, how do you fast, how do you treat a neighbor, a spouse, a stranger? In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gives his companions a short answer about the prayer: pray as you have seen me praying. Watch the hands.
screen: `NOBODY LEARNS A KNOT FROM A PARAGRAPH.`
`PRAY AS YOU HAVE SEEN ME PRAY.`

segments.voice: Wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah. And I testify that Muhammad is His messenger. The Qur'an says it in nearly the same words, in Pickthall's translation: "Muhammad is the messenger of Allah." First, the word. A rasul is a messenger, one who is sent. Risalah is what he carries: the message, and the mission of carrying it. In the second sentence, Muslims testify that this man was sent, and that what he brought came from beyond him. Second, the message came with a life attached. The Qur'an doesn't hand over a book and leave. It points at a person: "Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example." The way he prayed, ate, argued, forgave and grieved became the sunnah, his way, the pattern Muslims look to for how the first sentence gets lived on an ordinary day. Third, a messenger and not more. The Qur'an tells him to say: "I am only a mortal like you." Muslims honor him deeply, and worship only God. The two sentences keep that line clean: the first is about who is worshiped, the second about who shows the way. Fourth, he is one in a line. The Qur'an names earlier messengers, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and describes believers who make no distinction between any of them. It calls Muhammad the seal of the prophets. So the second sentence isn't a footnote to the first. It answers the question the first one raises. One God, yes. And here is how people have seen it lived, by a man who slept, walked to market, and asked for help like anyone else.

The practice: choose one sunnah to follow today. Settle, and breathe. Here are a few small things the hadith collections describe him doing. Beginning a meal by saying bismillah, in the name of God, and eating with the right hand. Greeting people with peace, those you know and those you don't. Visiting someone who is sick. Pick one that fits your day, whether you're Muslim or simply curious how it feels. Then spend the rest of the sit walking through exactly where and when you'll do it. The bell holds the time.
Risalah. The message, and the mission of the one sent with it: the second half of the testimony. Today's word.

Your line: he shows the way. Today, do the one sunnah you chose, and notice whether it changes the moment around it. Tomorrow, what happens when someone says both sentences for the first time. Day one thousand sixty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims learn the sunnah, the Prophet's way, from the hadith collections and from teachers and parents, and many try to follow it in small daily habits as well as in the prayer.

fork.setup: the companions want to know exactly how to pray. what does the Prophet tell them?
options: read the instructions I'll write down.
pray as you have seen me praying.
pray however feels right to you.
fork.reveal: Sahih al-Bukhari records it: the prayer was taught by watching him, the way a knot is taught by watching hands.

original.note: the message, the mission; the one who carries it is the رَسُول (ra-SOOL), messenger.

trapdoor: what you thought: "messenger" means someone who delivered a book and left.
what it means: he carried the message and showed it, in a life Muslims call the sunnah.
what a scholar hears: 18:110 and 33:21 hold both sides at once: only a mortal, and the good example.
recall: a charity that keeps flowing after you die
character: the way a person habitually is
